forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: West Suffolk Council used £60.6m of its own cash instead of loans to fund projects at 30 June 2026
news_drafts.lead:
West Suffolk Council had used £60,634,266 of its own cash to pay for capital spending (money spent on things that last, such as buildings, roads, vehicles and equipment) at 30 June 2026, rather than taking out loans, according to a treasury management report (how a council borrows, invests its spare cash and manages the risks of both) referred from the Cabinet to full Council on 13 October.

This is known as internal borrowing: using the council's own cash reserves instead of a loan, which saves interest but uses up the cushion. The report says the council's total borrowing, counting both internal and external loans, is expected to increase over the full financial year.

That expected rise comes even though repayments of loans from the Public Works Loan Board (the government's lending arm for councils, run by the Treasury, and where most council borrowing comes from) are continuing as planned. The Cabinet considered the report on 15 September 2026, and the papers give the position as of the end of June, the first quarter of the financial year.

news_drafts.headline: West Suffolk's audit qualification will persist until £7.8m property revaluation completes
news_drafts.lead: West Suffolk moved out of audit limbo this year when its external auditor, Ernst & Young, issued a qualified opinion on the 2024-25 accounts—the first audit assurance in three years following the national local audit backlog. The auditor reports no concerns with the council's value-for-money arrangements. However, the qualification cannot be lifted until the council completes revaluation of £7.8 million in property assets last valued in 2022-23. Once revalued, a further two-year lag in the accounts will follow before an unqualified opinion can be issued, putting full clearance at 2027-28 at the earliest. The council signed its 2025-26 draft accounts a month ahead of the extended statutory deadline, and the auditor expects to issue an opinion well in advance of the January 2027 backstop date.

findings.headline: Capital projects are being timed to be delivered by Local Government Reorganisation vesting day
findings.detail: The COO explained that the capital programme was considered in the context of the impending LGR and the need to deliver projects by vesting day.
findings.matters: LGR timing creates a hard deadline for project completion that may conflict with delivery schedules; the use of vesting day as a project deadline affects which council completes which projects and the financing of schemes through the transition
findings.figures: No vesting date specified in this document
findings.quote: capital programme had been considered in the context of LGR and the delivery of the projects therein by vesting day

findings.headline: Capital project delays attributed to planning process issues with Rougham Hill redevelopment; carried-forward budgets subject to inflation cost pressure
findings.detail: The COO noted delays in delivery from various causes including planning process issues with the Rougham Hill redevelopment. In response to concerns about inflation impact on projects carried forward, the COO stressed all projects had been thoroughly considered.
findings.matters: Project delays drive cost inflation and change borrowing timing and amounts; understanding whether delays are systemic or project-specific affects forecasting of actual capital spend and its financing
findings.quote: delays relating to Rougham Hill redevelopment had resulted from issues arising from the planning process rather than any lack of commitment to the project

findings.headline: Capital programme consistently carries forward budgets annually, resulting in underspend
findings.detail: The Committee were assured that projects routinely span multiple years and budgets are carried forward each year as a result. This practice results in an underspend on the annual capital programme, described as normal practice.
findings.matters: Finance directors track whether councils deliver planned capital investment; consistent annual underspend indicates either over-optimistic planning or delivery capacity constraints, both affecting borrowing needs and investment outcomes
findings.quote: Therefore, carry forwards of capital budgets were considered annually, thereby resulting in an underspend on the capital programme.

findings.headline: Internal borrowing £60,634,266 with overall borrowing expected to increase across full year
findings.detail: Internal borrowing stood at £60,634,266 as at 30 June 2026. The council expects total borrowing (external and internal combined) to increase over the full financial year, despite planned PWLB repayments continuing.
findings.matters: When internal borrowing grows while external debt is being repaid, it typically signals cash outflows are outpacing income, requiring the council to draw on reserves rather than generate cash for additional borrowing.
findings.quote: The Council's level of internal borrowing being £60,634,266 as at 30 June 2026. Overall borrowing (total of both external and internal) is expected to increase over the full financial year.

findings.headline: External borrowing reduced by £125,000 in first quarter, reflecting PWLB loan repayment
findings.detail: External borrowing as at 30 June 2026 was £8,875,000, down £125,000 from 1 April 2026. The reduction reflects scheduled repayments on the council's recent Public Works Loan Board £10 million 40-year loan, indicating the planned repayment schedule is being maintained.
findings.matters: Lenders and peer councils monitor whether councils meet PWLB repayment obligations and manage large borrowing facilities responsibly.
findings.figures: External borrowing £8,875,000 (30 June 2026); reduction of £125,000 from 1 April 2026; from £10m PWLB 40-year loan
findings.quote: External borrowing as at 30 June 2026 was £8,875,000, a reduction of £125,000 from 1 April 2026 (relates to the repayment plan for the recent Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) £10 million 40-year loan)

daily_post.headline: The council's wholly-owned housing company, Barley Homes Group Limited, received an unqualified audit opinion for 2024-2025.
daily_post.lead: The council's ability to use its housing company for housing delivery and economic development depends on sound controls and clean audit opinions. An unqualified opinion provides assurance that the subsidiary can function as intended despite audit issues…
